title: 75-year-old Canadian woman charged in Florida for illegally voting in 3 federal polls
text: Canadian woman Christiane Vinette Young charged in US over illegal voting. A 75-year-old Canadian national has been charged in Florida with allegedly voting in three US federal elections despite not being a US citizen. Christiane Vinette Young is accused of casting ballots in the 2024 general election, the 2022 general election and the 2022 primary election, US Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe announced. Federal prosecutors said Young was unlawfully present in the United States and knew she was not a US citizen when she voted. Young faces three counts of voting by an alien. If convicted on all charges, she could receive a maximum sentence of three years in federal prison. The case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, with assistance from the Florida Department of Law Enforcement and the Lee County Supervisor of Elections. Assistant US Attorney Benjamin S. Winter is prosecuting the case. Young's case comes alongside separate federal charges against two non-US citizens in Pennsylvania over alleged election-related offences. Cliff Sanon, 39, a Haitian national living in Philadelphia, has been charged with allegedly submitting a fraudulent voter registration application in February 2026. Prosecutors allege the application was among eight fraudulent registrations and that Sanon also voted in the November 2022 election. He faces a maximum of five years in prison if convicted. Dilea Ochoa-Perez, 43, a Mexican national living in Coatesville, Pennsylvania, has been charged with two counts of voting as an alien. Prosecutors allege she voted in Chester County in the November 2022 and November 2024 general elections. She faces a maximum of two years in prison if convicted. You use AI every day. A communication from the secretary general of the Supreme Court to the committee said the proposal for an informal discussion by the joint committee to examine Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024, and the UT Laws (Amendments Bill, 2024) on the subject of simultaneous elections with Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and other judges on Oct 6 was discussed among the senior judges. title: GMC polls: Turncoat corporators political future hangs in balance
text: Guntur : Political uncertainty is mounting among former YSRCP corporators who crossed over to the Telugu Desam Party (TDP) after the last general elections, with questions over whether they will secure tickets in the forthcoming local body elections looming large. Around 23 YSRCP corporators, including then deputy mayor Shaik Sajila, shifted their allegiance to the TDP soon after the TDP-led NDA emerged victorious in the general elections in 2024. They have also helped dethrone the YSRCP mayor and got senior TDP leader Kovelamudi Ravindra (Nani) elected as mayor. However, the prospects of turncoat corporators getting renominated from TDP in the next municipal elections look very bleak as the competition is heavy within the ruling coalition. The GMC had 57 divisions when elections were held in March 2021. YSRCP won 44 seats, while TDP secured nine, Jana Sena Party two and independents two. Subsequently, an independent corporator joined YSRCP, taking its strength to 45. The political equations have changed considerably since then, with a section of YSRCP corporators moving to the TDP following the change of govt. Many of them are now seeking to continue their political careers from the TDP platform. The latest delimitation has added another layer of complexity. The number of GMC divisions has been increased from 57 to 76, redrawing ward boundaries and creating new local-level equations. The key issue for the former YSRCP corporators is whether they will be accommodated in the new ward structure and given an opportunity to contest as TDP nominees. Sources said that local TDP leaders and long-time activists are strongly opposing the fielding of former corporators in the next elections. Although the number of divisions increased substantially, the pressure from Janasena and BJP might eat into the newly created divisions. Sources said that Janasena has requested allocation of at least 20-25 divisions while BJP sought 10 divisions. A five-member committee comprising union minister Pemmasani Chandrasekhar, local legislators, in-charge minister Kandula Durgesh and BJP district president has completed initial discussions on the seat-sharing issue and decided to meet once again next week to identify the strength of each party before going for selection of the candidates. Sources said that Janasena is believed to be pressing for a major share in the divisions in view of a considerable Kapu population in all the three assembly constituencies in the city and also its strong base among the youth. Sources, however, said that TDP leaders are not willing to part with a huge number of seats, saying that their cadre is also keen to take the field. The long-time activists, division in-charges and those who lost the previous election are exerting pressure on the party legislators to ensure tickets to contest. In the given situation, sources said that very few former YSRCP corporators are expected to get fielded in the next elections. âIt will be extremely difficult for us to pick up the former corporators as our nominees as there are huge number of aspirants from our own cadre. We are under no obligation to entertain their demands as they have joined the party unconditionally,â said a TDP legislator from the city. title: Tawde tells cadre to plug organisational gaps
text: Vinod Tawde Lucknow: With an eye on the Assembly elections, BJP on Thursday kick-started its poll preparations, with national general secretary and UP incharge Vinod Tawde directing party members to devise region-specific strategies and plug organisational gaps believed to have contributed to the partyâs reduced tally in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. At a high-level meeting at the state BJP headquarters in Lucknow, Tawde and four co-incharges -- Jagdish Patel, Medha Kulkarni, Pradeep Kumar Verma and Anant Ojha -- reviewed the situation across regions and discussed preparations for the upcoming Rajya Sabha and MLC elections. They separately met chief minister Yogi Adityanath and deputy CMs Keshav Prasad Maurya and Brajesh Pathak before holding deliberations with regional presidents and regional incharges. Though BJP did not officially disclose the agenda, sources said Tawde sought detailed feedback on the political and organisational situation in each region and asked senior members to formulate strategies keeping local realities in mind. Stressing the need for course correction ahead of the Assembly polls, he reportedly told organisational members to address weaknesses that surfaced during the 2024 LS elections. The meeting also had detailed discussions on elections to 10 Rajya Sabha seats. Party leaders assessed BJPâs numerical strength in the Assembly and discussed prospective candidates. The review comes after the state unit forwarded a panel of names to the central leadership, which will take the final call on nominations. Preparations for elections to 11 teachersâ and graduatesâ MLC constituencies were also reviewed. BJP has already announced its candidates for those contests. Later in the evening, Tawde and the co-incharges left for Varanasi, where they are scheduled to participate in programmes marking Gandhi Jayanti. Tawde is expected to hold a review meeting with Kashi region functionaries during the visit. title: From Bihar Win to UP Battle: Tawde Leads BJPâs Poll Playbook
text: Vinod Tawde Lucknow: BJP national general secretary and Uttar Pradesh incharge Vinod Tawde âs visit to Lucknow on Thursday, his fifth to the state in less than a month after getting the charge, appears to be more than a routine organisational exercise. Tawdeâs role is significant since he is considered as one of the key strategists of BJPâs win in Bihar polls last year. With UP Assembly elections just months away, Tawde is increasingly emerging as a key strategist tasked with sharpening the BJPâs organisational machinery and strengthening its electoral prospects against an aggressive opposition led by the Samajwadi Party and its ally Congress . Tawde signalled this approach from the outset. During his first visit to Lucknow on Sept 5, he reportedly advised party workers against putting up oversized hoardings or organising a grand welcome, sending a clear message that the focus should be on strengthening the organisation and preparing for the elections rather than on symbolism. The move was notable because it was in contrast to the elaborate receptions often accorded to senior BJP mmebers, including state party chief Pankaj Chaudhary, during their initial visits to Lucknow and other parts of Uttar Pradesh. The restraint reflected Tawdeâs preference for a work-centric approach as the party gears up for the high-stakes electoral battle ahead. Sources said that in the Thursday meeting, Tawde expressed concern over the oppositionâs PDA pitch which impacted BJP in 2024 Lok Sabha elections. A senior UP BJP member said the party is giving stress on mobilisation of workers at the grassroots and bolstering coordination between the organisation and govt. Tawde has been holding one-to-one discussions with organisational members and CM Yogi and deputy CMs Keshav Prasad Maurya and Brajesh Pathak. During his second visit to Lucknow on Sept 11, where he was accompanied by national general secretary (organisation) BL Santhosh, Tawde held high-profile review meetings which were attended by Keshav Maurya and Brajesh Pathak, ministers and key organisational heads. Having done his ground work, Tawde embarked on a region-wise organisational assessment on Sept 17, beginning from Gorakhpur. Sources said he engaged with grassroots cadre and UP BJP politicians to assess legislatorsâ performance and collect feedback on potential candidates for the Assembly elections. Tawde accompanied BJP chief Nitin Nabin to Meerut and Saharanpur on Sept 21 and 22 where they held closed-door meetings with the regional leaders and party representatives, including MPs, MLAs and MLCs, in the west UP region. Tawde is next scheduled to participate in the high-level organisational meeting in Mathura on Oct 3 and 4. BJP sources said Tawde is trying to replicate Bihar poll model, which he spearheaded as the state in-charge since 2022, in UP elections. Tawde is recognised as one of the frontline organisational members who led NDA to win 30 out of 40 Lok Sabha seats in Bihar in the 2024 elections. The strategy was repeated in the 2025 Bihar assembly elections. A senior UP BJP member, who camped in Bihar during the assembly elections, said the strategy prioritised micro-management and grassroots alignment. Tawde is learnt to have made at least 15 visits to Bihar in the run-up to the state polls. title: US Supreme Court rejects Trump-backed Missouri congressional map for third time
text: More than 1 million Missouri voters affected (Visitors at the US Supreme Court. Reuters image) The US Supreme Court on Friday rejected an attempt to use a new Missouri congressional map backed by President Donald Trump, potentially bringing an end to a long-running redistricting dispute as absentee voting gets underway in the state. The justices halted a ruling by a federal appeals court that would have revived the Republican-friendly map for the November midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. The Supreme Court instead allowed a decision by the Missouri Supreme Court to stand. The state court had ruled earlier this month that a citizen petition prevents the new congressional map from being used unless it is first approved by voters in a November referendum. The decision means Missouri voters will use the same congressional districts that were in place for the 2022 and 2024 elections. Why the Supreme Court rejected the new map Republicans had hoped the new House map, which was already used during Missouri's August primaries, would help them gain an additional seat as part of a nationwide redistricting effort backed by Trump ahead of the midterm elections. A panel of the 8th US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled Monday that changing congressional districts between the primary and general elections would violate the US Constitution. The panel directed a district judge to prevent Missouri from using any map other than the new districts. However, the appeals court delayed the order from taking effect until the following Monday, giving Missouri time to appeal to the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court's latest decision now leaves the earlier Missouri Supreme Court ruling in place, meaning the new map cannot be used for the November general election unless voters approve it in the referendum. More than 1 million Missouri voters affected The legal dispute has created uncertainty for more than 1 million potential Missouri voters, nearly one in four statewide, who were shifted from one congressional district to another under the new map. The changes also meant some voters faced different candidates on their ballots. Absentee voting began Tuesday under the 2022 congressional districts, although some local election officials had urged voters to wait because of the uncertainty over which map would ultimately be used. With Friday's Supreme Court decision, voters will use the existing congressional boundaries for the November election. How Trump's redistricting push reshaped Kansas City Republicans currently hold six of Missouri's eight US House seats. At the urging of Trump and Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe, Missouri lawmakers last September approved revised congressional districts intended to help Republicans win seven seats in the midterms. The new map made major changes to a Kansas City-based district held by longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver. Under the revised boundaries, parts of Kansas City were shifted into neighbouring districts represented by Republican incumbents. The remainder of Cleaver's 5th Congressional District was extended eastward into rural Republican areas. An Associated Press estimate found that about 59% of potential voters in the district were new under the revised boundaries. The changes also affected voters in most of Missouri's other congressional districts. Cleaver was unopposed in the Democratic primary, while Republican state Sen. Rick Brattin won a six-way Republican primary under the revised map. Both remain the candidates for the November general election despite the congressional boundaries reverting to their previous lines. Brattin was among the plaintiffs in a federal lawsuit that resulted in the 8th Circuit ruling and the latest two appeals to the Supreme Court. Republican Rep. Bob Onder and two other voters were also plaintiffs. Missouri redistricting triggered multiple legal challenges At least 16 lawsuits have been filed in state and federal courts over Missouri's congressional redistricting. The dispute has become the longest and most complex among roughly a dozen states that sought to alter their US House districts over the past year. The new map survived most of the legal challenges, including cases arguing that mid-decade redistricting violated the Missouri Constitution and that the revised districts failed to meet requirements for compactness. In one case, the Missouri Supreme Court allowed the new districts to be used while election officials verified signatures on a petition seeking to put the map before voters in a statewide referendum. Republican Secretary of State Denny Hoskins waited until the legal deadline on August 4, the day the new districts were used in the primary, to reject the petition. He argued that referendum petitions were not permitted for congressional redistricting. The Missouri Supreme Court later ruled on September 3 that the referendum petition was valid. It ordered Hoskins not to use the new map and directed election officials to use the districts adopted in 2022 following the last census. Supreme Court has intervened repeatedly The US Supreme Court allowed the Missouri Supreme Court's September 3 ruling to stand on September 8. Minutes later, however, US District Judge Stephen Clark issued a conflicting order favouring the new congressional map. The Supreme Court blocked Clark's order from taking effect on September 10. That same day, the Missouri Supreme Court temporarily held Hoskins in contempt after he told local election authorities to use the new map following Clark's order. The dispute continued when the 8th Circuit considered an appeal of Clark's blocked order and ruled Monday in favour of the Trump-backed map. That ruling led to the latest appeal before the US Supreme Court. Friday's decision is the third time the Supreme Court has intervened to block efforts to use the new congressional map, leaving Missouri's previous congressional boundaries in place for the November midterm election. title: $888 million for ads: US Republicans ramp up sends to defend 39 House seats once deemed 'safe'
text: Republicans hold a 218-214 House majority, with one independent caucusing with them and two vacancies; Democrats need four seats to take control. US Republicans are pouring money into more than three dozen US House races previously considered safe for the party, with Republican groups reserving $888 million in advertising for the coming weeks, compared with $666 million for Democrats, according to AdImpact. Since September 1, major Republican groups and megadonors have begun spending in at least 39 House races where they had not previously deployed money this election cycle, a Reuters review found. Republican-leaning super PACs have also outspent Democrats almost 2-to-1 since Labor Day, spending about $309.7 million compared with $174.2 million, Federal Election Commission data shows, as cited by Reuters. What happened at 'safe' seats? Many of the districts remain Republican strongholds, with candidates still leading in public polls and several having backed Donald Trump by double-digit margins in 2024. But Republican leaders have warned campaigns that internal polling shows they cannot assume victory, according to people familiar with the party's thinking, quoted by Reuters. Economic pressures, including rising fuel, energy and fertiliser costs, are also hurting traditionally Republican areas, while party strategists are concerned voters could use the November 3 election to register dissatisfaction with Trump's policies. âRepublicans are playing defense in some of the strongholds that they're used to not having to worry about,â said Republican strategist Ron Bonjean. âWe're in this crucial period in the last 30 days where candidates have to really make a case, given how tough the headwinds are,â said Kevin Madden, a former adviser to Mitt Romney. Republicans say the additional spending is intended to protect their House majority. âRepublicans are deploying our massive war chest to drive voters to the polls and supercharge our candidates,â said Natalie Baldassarre, national press secretary for the Republican National Committee. Republicans hold a 218-214 House majority, with one independent caucusing with them and two vacancies. Democrats need to gain at least four seats to take control. One example is Wisconsin Republican Bryan Steil, whose district backed Trump by about 4.5 percentage points in 2024. Conservative super PACs have put $1.5 million into his race this month, their first spending there this cycle. In Texas, Republican groups have spent about $2 million since September 5 to support Representative Monica De La Cruz, whose district Trump won by 18 points. Cook Political Report moved the race from âlean Republicanâ to âtossupâ on Friday. title: BJPâs 2027 poll blueprint set to take shape at Mathura meet on Oct 3-4
text: Lucknow: With the battle for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections beginning to take shape, BJP is set to unveil the broad contours of its electoral strategy at a crucial two-day organisational meeting to be held in Mathura on Oct 3 and 4. The meeting is expected to bring together the partyâs top brass amid growing signs of an aggressive contest with Samajwadi Party and Congress. The meeting will be attended by BJP national president Nitin Nabin , national general secretary and UP in charge Vinod Tawde , chief minister Yogi Adityanath , UP BJP chief Pankaj Chaudhary , besides all state vice-presidents, general secretaries and key organisational leaders from six regions. While the official agenda is yet to be released, party insiders said the deliberations would focus on assessing the ground-level political situation, identifying challenges posed by the opposition and finalising the framework of campaigns that the party would take up in the run-up to the polls. âWe have been asked to keep all engagements aside and attend the Mathura meeting. The detailed agenda is expected shortly,â a senior BJP functionary said. The choice of Mathura is significant and politically loaded. Considered one of the ideological centres of the Hindutva movement, the city has increasingly occupied a central place in BJPâs political discourse. Party strategists view the Braj region not merely as an electoral battleground but as a crucial pillar of the larger narrative that seeks to consolidate voters across caste lines under an overarching Hindu identity. The meeting comes at a time when BJP is recalibrating its ideological messaging after the completion of Ram Temple project in Ayodhya. It will be the first time in decades that the party will fight a UP Assembly election without Ram Mandir construction issue as a plank. Political observers say BJP is looking to expand the Hindutva narrative beyond Ayodhya, with Mathura emerging as the next major focal point. The shift assumes significance as Ayodhya has recently witnessed controversy over alleged theft of temple donations, leading to changes in the temple management structure. Senior BJP functionaries have been underscoring the importance of developing Mathura into a major religious and cultural hub. Yogi has made several visits to the district in recent months to review development projects and pilgrimage infrastructure. The symbolism is not lost on the party leadership too. Nitin Nabin chose Mathura for his first visit after taking charge as BJP national president earlier this year, while Pankaj Chaudhary offered prayers at Banke Bihari temple soon after assuming office as the state BJP chief. Beyond symbolism, the Braj region holds electoral value. Spread across 19 organisational districts, the region has traditionally been a BJP stronghold. However, the partyâs performance dipped in the 2024 Lok Sabha elections, raising concerns within the organisation. After winning 12 of the regionâs 13 parliamentary seats in 2019, BJPâs tally fell to eight in 2024, prompting the leadership to intensify political and organisational outreach. The assembly numbers tell a similar story. BJP won 53 of the regionâs 65 assembly seats in 2022, down from 57 in 2017 when the party stormed to power with a record mandate and Yogi Adityanath became chief minister. Against this backdrop, the Mathura conclave is expected to serve not only as a strategy session for the 2027 elections but also as a signal that BJP intends to make Braj a key theatre in both its electoral and ideological campaign in the months ahead. title: Trumpâs own America.gov chatbot contradicts US president on 2020 polls, climate
text: Trumpâs new AI chatbot pushes back on claims about polls, climate, salary The AI-powered America.gov website launched by US President Donald Trump on Tuesday gave factual answers to several politically sensitive questions, including some that contradicted claims made by the president. According to Associated Press, the website, launched to make government information and services easier to access, initially answered questions about the 2020 election, Trumpâs possible 2028 presidential bid, climate change and presidential salaries. On the 2020 election, the chatbot said: âOfficial federal sources do not show that widespread fraud changed the 2020 presidential election outcome. title: UK PM Andy Burnham rules out early general polls, says âno election anytime soonâ
text: UK PM Andy Burnham UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham has ruled out calling an early general election, saying his focus is on tackling the cost of living and supporting businesses rather than putting the country through another election campaign. Iâm focused on the job as prime minister, doing what I said I would do.â Burnham was also asked whether a general election would be held next May alongside council elections in the East Midlands. âNo,â he replied. âNot having a general election.â The comments come amid speculation that the government could call an early election, with reports that some advisers had been considering a poll as early as next year. Polling in recent weeks has shown a change in Labour's position since Burnham became prime minister in July, although Reform UK and the Conservatives have also remained competitive. title: Mayor poll row: Audit flags inaction against Anil Masih
text: Masih was the presiding officer for the Jan 30, 2024, mayoral election. CHANDIGARH: Nearly two and a half years after Supreme Court intervened in the Chandigarh mayoral election controversy, the director general of audit (central), Chandigarh, has flagged govtâs âinactionâ regarding the implementation of SCâs directions against then-presiding officer Anil Masih. The audit seeks to know what action was taken by govt and Chandigarh Municipal Corporation following the apex courtâs judgment and why no action was taken at govt level. The audit enquiry, dated June 2, 2026, seeks details of action under Section 33(2) of Punjab Municipal Corporation Act and asks whether Masih, a nominated BJP councillor, was a public servant and whether his services could continue after the alleged misconduct. Masih was the presiding officer for the Jan 30, 2024, mayoral election. During counting, he invalidated eight votes cast in favour of AAP-Congress alliance candidate Kuldeep Kumar. Supreme Court examined the ballots and video footage, and found that all eight votes were valid. It quashed the election result that had declared BJPâs Manoj Kumar Sonkar the winner and declared Kumar the validly elected mayor. The controversy escalated after video footage from the counting room showed Masih marking the ballots as invalid. âSupreme Court held that a fit and proper case was made out for invoking its jurisdiction under Section 340 of CrPC in respect of Masihâs conduct and directed its registrar (judicial) to issue him a showcause notice,â noted the audit report. In its response, Chandigarh municipal corporation said the matter has been âreferred to the higher authorityâ via a letter dated June 3, 2026, for further action. The audit observation would remain pending until the final outcome / decision in the case. The audit document records that the final reply is still awaited. Chandigarh-based social activist RK Garg said, âTwo years on and no action in the case. It shows poorly on the administration that the issue had to be raised by the CAG in the audit.â The controversy led to a change in the way Chandigarh elects its mayor. In 2025, UT administrator approved an amendment to Regulation 6 of the Chandigarh Municipal Corporation (Procedure and Conduct of Business) Regulations, replacing the traditional secret-ballot system with voting by show of hands. The new system was used for the Jan 2026 mayoral election. title: Jail, isolation, crackdown: Why Pakistanâs establishment has failed to break Imran Khan
text: Former Pakistan PM Imran Khan has been incarcerated since 2023 (File photo) Islamabad had prepared for another confrontation. Roads were blocked, security forces deployed and Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) supporters were expected to march towards the capital demanding the release of their jailed leader, Imran Khan . Then, days before the September 27 protest, PTI postponed the march until October 4, temporarily easing the pressure on the government. But the roads can be reopened and the barricades removed. The political problem surrounding Imran Khan is proving harder to clear. The former prime minister has now spent more than three years behind bars. The establishment has used imprisonment, restrictions on his contact with the outside world, scores of legal cases and a crackdown on his supporters. Yet none of it has so far succeeded in removing Imran Khan from the centre of Pakistan's politics. PTI-backed independents won the largest number of directly elected national assembly seats in the 2024 general election, and his supporters continue to mobilise around demands for his release. The postponed Islamabad march is therefore less an end to the latest confrontation than another pause in a political standoff that has survived elections, convictions and imprisonment. How Imran Khan got here Imran Khan retired from international cricket in 1992, shortly after leading Pakistan to its first and, so far, only 50-over Cricket World Cup title. Four years later, in 1996, he formally entered politics by founding the PTI. His political breakthrough finally came after the 2018 general election, when the PTI emerged as the single-largest party and he became prime minister. His rise to power was widely seen by rivals and analysts as having benefited from the backing of Pakistanâs military, the countryâs most powerful institution, although both Khan and the military denied that the army had helped bring him to power. That relationship subsequently deteriorated. In April 2022, the opposition brought a parliamentary no-confidence vote against Imran Khan, which he lost and was thus removed from office. He has since faced more than 100 cases, many involving corruption allegations. Several of his convictions have been overturned, suspended or otherwise challenged, while he has consistently denied wrongdoing. Imran Khan was imprisoned in August 2023 and has remained behind bars since then. Yet his incarceration has done little to diminish his presence in Pakistanâs public life or erase him from the public consciousness. Why Imran Khan matters Thanks to his cricket career, Imran Khan was already a well-known public figure before entering politics. Following his retirement, he gained further goodwill by giving Pakistan its first specialised cancer hospital, the Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital, named after his mother, in Lahore. The hospital opened in 1994. That personal following later became the foundation of a political movement, the PTI, that presented him as an outsider challenging Pakistanâs established political order. In a country where civilian politics has long been shaped by the Bhutto-Zardari and Sharif families, Imran Khan offered voters a figure outside the traditional political dynasties. His image as a retired cricket captain with no family legacy in politics helped distinguish him from the established political class. Imran Khan: From cricket captain to PM to inmate His prime ministership brought him further visibility and established him as a central figure in Pakistanâs civilian politics. And therein lies his significance: an outsider who challenged Pakistanâs established political dynasties, became prime minister, and later fell out with the military establishment before being jailed. How state failed to marginalise Imran Khan politically Pakistanâs 2024 general election offered the clearest indication that Imran Khanâs imprisonment had not erased his political relevance. Despite the PTI being stripped of its election symbol and Imran Khan remaining in prison, PTI-backed independents won 92 directly elected National Assembly seats â more than candidates backed by any other political grouping. While that result did not bring the party back to power, it showed that his absence from the ballot did not translate into the disappearance of his support. However, the outcome should not have been a surprise. In October 2022, just months after his ouster as prime minister, Imran Khan contested by-elections in seven of eight National Assembly constituencies voting on October 16. He won six of the seven seats he contested, while the Pakistan Peopleâs Party won the other two constituencies. He then won another by-election in Kurram on October 30, taking his tally of by-election victories that month to seven. The by-election results offered an early indication that removing Imran Khan from office had not dented his electoral support. The 2024 elections reinforced that point, showing that his imprisonment and the restrictions placed on the PTI had not eliminated its support among voters. Imran Khan: PTI's 'red line' As its founder and most prominent face, PTI has repeatedly described Imran Khan as its âred line.â The phrase took on greater significance after his arrest on May 9, 2023, when Pakistan witnessed widespread rioting and arson by PTI supporters. Protesters targeted government buildings and military installations, including the residence of a corps commander in Lahore and the armyâs general headquarters in Rawalpindi. The events marked a dramatic escalation in the confrontation between Imran Khan and the military establishment. They also demonstrated why the PTI has continued to place him at the centre of its politics: attempts to remove him from the political arena have not removed the attachment to him among a significant section of the partyâs supporters. Since his incarceration, the party has repeatedly mobilised in Islamabad, demanding his release. The federal governmentâs frustration with these protests was evident ahead of the recently postponed Islamabad march, when interior minister Mohsin Naqvi spoke of the need to find a âpermanent solutionâ to the PTIâs repeated demonstrations in the capital. âThis time we will find a permanent solution; we will not leave it halfway,â Naqvi said. Therefore, Imran Khan remains the PTIâs âred lineâ â one reason efforts to marginalise him politically have so far struggled to succeed. The 'persecution' of Imran Khan Imran Khanâs prolonged imprisonment has also strengthened a persecution narrative around him. His party and supporters have consistently argued that the numerous cases against him are politically motivated and intended to keep him out of politics. Pakistani authorities have rejected those allegations. The fact that more than 100 cases have been brought against him, his disqualification by the Election Commission in 2022, and the restrictions imposed on the PTI ahead of the 2024 general elections have only strengthened that narrative among his supporters. Main legal cases against Imran Khan The conditions of his imprisonment at Rawalpindiâs Adiala Jail have added another dimension to the persecution narrative. In December 2025, UN Special Rapporteur on torture Alice Jill Edwards raised concerns over reports that Khan was being held in conditions falling below international standards for humane and dignified detention. The communication cited allegations of prolonged solitary confinement, restricted access to the outside world and inadequate ventilation. Edwards subsequently urged Pakistani authorities to end his reported solitary confinement and ensure that his detention conditions complied with international standards, warning that the reported conditions could amount to torture or other inhuman or degrading treatment. The Pakistani establishment has succeeded in keeping Imran Khan behind bars. But with so many eyes on his case, it has not succeeded in making his political relevance disappear. Imran Khan: A case that resonates beyond politics The controversy surrounding Imran Khanâs imprisonment has increasingly extended beyond politics and Pakistan, as his cricketing legacy has kept his case in the international spotlight. Former international cricket captains have appealed to Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharifâs government over Khanâs treatment and access to medical care. In August, 21 former captains urged the government to ensure âhumane treatment and proper medical careâ for their former on-field rival. Matters almost came to a head during the recent England-Pakistan Test series. During the second Test at Lordâs, the Pakistan Cricket Board reportedly considered not sending its players back onto the field after the lunch break after Sky Sports aired an interview with Imran Khanâs sons, Kasim and Suleiman. The PCB ultimately returned to the field and lodged a complaint with the broadcaster. The episode underscored how Imran Khanâs imprisonment continues to attract attention beyond Pakistan and outside politics. The stateâs struggle to marginalise Imran Khan Every time the PTI has marched on Islamabad, the Pakistan government has responded by fortifying the capital, blocking entry routes and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel. Ahead of the September 27 march, authorities deployed thousands of security personnel and erected extensive barricades and roadblocks around Islamabad. The crackdown extended to Imran Khanâs family too, with his three sisters detained ahead of the now-postponed march. Such measures may prevent protesters from reaching Islamabad, but they have not stopped the PTI from returning to the streets with the same central demand: Imran Khanâs release. The state has managed to contain individual protests, but each confrontation has been followed by another, keeping his imprisonment at the centre of Pakistanâs politics. By isolating him in prison and cracking down on his family and party, the Pakistani authorities have sought to contain Imran Khanâs political influence. So far, however, his electoral support, PTIâs continued mobilisation and the attention surrounding his imprisonment show that those measures have not removed him from the countryâs political contest. For now, Imran Khanâs ability to retain political relevance despite his imprisonment remains a significant feature of Pakistanâs politics. You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. title: FBI co-deputy director Andrew Bailey resigns after just over a year, says âreturning to family in Missouriâ
text: FBI co-deputy director Andrew Bailey FBI Co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey is stepping down from his post after just over a year at the US law enforcement agency, saying he is leaving to return to his family in Missouri. Bailey, a Republican ally of President Donald Trump, announced his resignation on Monday after joining the FBI from his position as Missouri attorney general. He served under FBI Director Kash Patel and was involved in investigations related to the 2020 US election. Writing on X (formerly Twitter), Bailey thanked Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Patel for the opportunity to serve at the FBI. âWith great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri,â Bailey wrote. He also expressed support for Patel, âI am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence.â Bailey was part of the FBI leadership overseeing day-to-day law enforcement operations. During his tenure, he helped manage the Trump administration's investigations into election-related issues and was present when FBI agents seized 2020 election ballots in Georgia earlier this year. The FBI has examined election records in several states but has not produced evidence supporting Trump's claims that widespread voter fraud caused his defeat in the 2020 presidential election. Bailey's departure comes about five weeks before the US midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. The Trump administration has also stepped up federal investigations into voting by non-US citizens ahead of the elections. The FBI's deputy director position has traditionally been held by career bureau officials and was considered a non-political role. Under Trump, political allies have been appointed to senior positions as the administration seeks to reshape the agency. Bailey initially served as co-deputy director alongside Dan Bongino, a former US Secret Service agent and conservative podcaster. Bongino left the FBI in January. He joined the FBI amid scrutiny of Patel's leadership, including the bureau's handling of investigative files involving late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, which created political pressure for the Trump administration and tensions within the Justice Department. title: Khairatabad seat declared vacant, bypoll battle set to begin
text: Hyderabad : Telangana is headed for another assembly by-election after the assembly secretariat formally declared the Khairatabad constituency vacant following the disqualification of Danam Nagender as its MLA. The vacancy was notified after the high courtâs order, which was recently upheld by the Supreme Court , paving the way for a bypoll in the constituency. Assembly secretary Rendla Thirupathi issued a gazette notification (C No. 210/Legn/2026) declaring the seat vacant. The notification, issued on Sept 26 and published on Monday, stated that Danam stands disqualified from the Telangana legislative assembly with effect from April 23, 2024, the date on which he filed his nomination as a Congress candidate for the 2024 Lok Sabha elections. âIn pursuance of the judgement by the Telangana high court in writ petition Nos. 8409 and 8647 of 2026 delivered on Sept 18, it is hereby notified that Danam Nagender, member of the legislative assembly, stands disqualified with effect from April 23, 2024, under the paragraph 2(1)(a) of the Tenth Schedule with Article 191(2) of the Constitution and the seat stands vacant with effect from April 23, 2024,â the gazette notification said. The declaration of vacancy clears the way for a by-election, which must be conducted within six months. Political circles expect the Khairatabad bypoll to be held alongside the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections before March 2027. This will be the third assembly by-election since the Congress came to power in Telangana in Dec 2023. Earlier bypolls were held in the Secunderabad Cantonment and Jubilee Hills constituencies following the deaths of the sitting MLAs, with the ruling Congress retaining both seats. Khairatabad, however, will mark the first assembly by-election in the state arising from the disqualification of an MLA. The development also assumes significance as the high court is yet to deliver its verdict in the defection cases involving nine other BRS legislators who switched allegiance. Sources said hearings in those cases are likely to resume in the second week of Oct. With a by-election now imminent, the Congress, BRS and BJP have begun preliminary preparations for the contest. Aspirants in all three parties have already stepped up efforts to secure nominations, though a clearer picture on candidates is expected only after the Election Commission of India announces the poll schedule for the Khairatabad by-election. title: 'Have you ever voted in US election?' 61-year-old Canadian citizen, US Green Card holder, detained at border, interrogated for 6 hours, made to sign removal order
text: 61-year-old Canadian woman who holds a US green card was detained at the border and was asked if she had ever voted in a US election. (CBC News) A 61-year-old Canadian citizen who has been living in the US for 14 years as a Green Card holder was detained by border officials and interrogated for hours about whether she ever voted for any US election. Paige Adamson told CBC News that she was on her way home from a birthday dinner in Tsawwassen, British Columbia, Canada, while her residence is in Point Roberts, Washington State, in the US. Two places at the center of the issue Point Roberts is a US territory, but it is physically cut off from the rest of Washington State by Canadian territory. So someone who lives in the United States in Point Roberts like Adamson can routinely have to cross into Canada and then re-enter the United States to go elsewhere in the region. Point Roberts is called a pene-exclave of the US state of Washington on the southernmost tip of the Tsawwassen peninsula, south of Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. 'Have you ever voted in a federal US election' Adamson told the CBC News that the first question she was asked was whether she ever voted in a federal US election. She regularly crossed the border but this was the first time she was stopped and asked this question. "They immediately said, 'Park over here and come into the office.'" Adamson said she told them that she never voted in the US but the Department of Homeland Security accused her of falsely claiming that she was a US citizen and that she voted. She was interrogated for six hours until after 2am and was made to sign documents before being admitted to the US. One of the documents CBC News reviewed said Adamson "must surrender for removal from the United States, if so ordered." The DHS said Adamson registered to vote in Whatcom County, Washington State. She also voted in Washington State's 2018 general election, it has been alleged. Adamson said she never voted in a federal election and did not remember ever voting in a state election but she received a ballot once and may have been registered. "I was basically treated like a criminal," she said, recounting the experience of the interrogation. These are evil, sick people.â âThe Iranian regime has murdered thousands of its own people, killed Americans overseas, executed acts of terrorism in the Strait of Hormuz, and launched indiscriminate attacks against its neighbors in the region," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in response to Pezeshkian's comments. âThe president is courageously ensuring that such an evil country never possesses a nuclear weapon, which will make the entire world safer and more stable,â Kelly said. title: âWake upâ: Iran releases 25-page letter urging US voters to reject Trump ahead of midterms
text: The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections Iranâs Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has made a direct appeal to American voters, urging them to reject President Donald Trump âs policies and âwrest control back from corrupt politiciansâ as the US heads towards its midterm elections. In a lengthy open letter addressed to the American public, the powerful Iranian military force argued that Washingtonâs war against Iran had failed to achieve its objectives and called for a change in US policy towards Tehran. The 25-page letter, released seven months after the US-Israel war against Iran began, seeks to draw a distinction between the American people and their government. The IRGC argues that ordinary Iranians and Americans share common interests and grievances, portraying both as victims of political leaders pursuing costly wars. It also urges Americans to oppose US support for Israel and foreign military interventions, while presenting peaceful coexistence between Washington and Tehran as possible if US policy changes. IRGC spokesman Gen Hossein Mohebbi reinforced the message at a news conference in Tehran on Tuesday, saying the only way for the conflict to end was for Washington to acknowledge defeat and withdraw. He urged Americans to reconsider their leadership and put pressure on the Trump administration, arguing that many US citizens remained unaware of what he described as the âharmsâ caused by its policies. Watch Trump Under Pressure From Veterans & Republican At Home As Iran War Drives Fuel Prices Higher The timing of the letter is significant. The letter was released about five weeks before the US midterm elections, with the IRGC describing the current period as a moment when the American political system is at its weakest. Mohebbi said he did not necessarily expect the letter to change the US administrationâs behaviour, but hoped American voters would hear its message. âWake upâ: Iran takes message to US voters The letter repeatedly attacks Trumpâs justification for the war, particularly his claim that Iranâs nuclear programme posed a threat that required military action. Tehran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons and maintains that its uranium enrichment programme has civilian purposes. âThe enemy [US] knows that Iran is not after nuclear weapons,â Mohebbi said, echoing the letterâs argument that Washington has used the nuclear issue as a pretext to pursue wider strategic and economic goals. The IRGC also claims that the US and Israel failed to achieve their stated objectives in the war. According to the letter, the targets shifted repeatedly after earlier goals, including regime change and partition of Iran, were not achieved. It lists objectives ranging from forcing Iranâs unconditional surrender and destroying its nuclear and missile programmes to taking control of the Strait of Hormuz. The letter declares Iran the victor, claiming that thousands of US and Israeli strikes damaged Iranian infrastructure but failed to accomplish their stated aims. It further claims that Iranian forces inflicted major losses on US military assets and severely damaged American bases across the region. These assertions are presented by the IRGC as evidence of a broader strategic defeat for Washington. The Strait of Hormuz features prominently in the letter and Mohebbiâs remarks. He rejected US claims that Iran had lost its leverage over the vital waterway, arguing that the movement of a limited number of vessels did not mean the strait was fully open. Oil exports through the waterway, however, have recovered substantially from the levels seen earlier in the conflict, according to figures cited in the supplied material. âDeath to Americaâ explained as attack on rulers The IRGC letter also attempts to explain one of the most recognisable slogans associated with Iranâs political system: âDeath to Americaâ. It argues that the phrase is directed at the US political establishment rather than the American population. ââDeath to Americaâ is a prayer for the eradication of the diabolical ruling elite whose seat of power is the White House,â the letter says. The document repeatedly contrasts the American public with Washingtonâs political leadership, claiming that taxpayers ultimately bear the financial burden of US wars. It asks Americans to question why their government continues to pursue military confrontation and warns of what it describes as the consequences of an ongoing conflict. The IRGCâs approach echoes Cold War-era efforts to reach an adversaryâs population directly. During the Vietnam War, Vietnamese broadcaster Trinh Thi Ngo, widely known as âHanoi Hannahâ, used English-language broadcasts to target American troops, urging them to question their government and the war. Her programmes highlighted US casualties, anti-war protests and reports critical of the conflict while presenting the Vietnamese sideâs narrative. Iran has similarly sought to communicate directly with Western audiences since the latest war began, using Iran-linked media and online networks, including English-language AI-generated videos, memes and short-form content. The IRGC letter now represents a much more formal version of that strategy: an attempt to speak past Washington and directly to American voters. For Tehran, the central message is that the war is not simply a military confrontation between two states, but a political choice that Americans themselves can challenge. Mohebbi urged them to put pressure on their government, while the letter concluded with a broader argument that Iranâs resistance had demonstrated the limits of American military power. Meanwhile, Iranâs economic pressures remain severe. The rial fell to a new record low on Tuesday, with traders in Tehran reportedly exchanging more than 2.5 million rials for one US dollar. title: How Joe Biden averted a wider war with Iran: Explained in 10 points
text: Ex-US President Joe Biden Former US Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk recounts how Bidenâs administration coordinated with Israel and regional allies to intercept Iranâs unprecedented missile attack in April 2024, while attempting to prevent the crisis from escalating into a regional war. The United States helped avert a wider Middle East conflict in April 2024 by coordinating an unprecedented multinational military effort to defend Israel against Iranâs missile and drone attack, according to former US Middle East coordinator Brett McGurk. In an account adapted from his forthcoming book Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages, published by The Atlantic, McGurk detailed how President Joe Biden navigated deteriorating relations with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, stalled hostage negotiations, Iranian-backed militia attacks and the threat of direct confrontation between Tehran and Tel Aviv. McGurk, who was closely involved in hostage negotiations alongside CIA Director William Burns, described how the US administration eventually used its military capabilities and diplomatic leverage to contain the Iranian attack and discourage Israel from launching an immediate counterstrike. Here is how Biden administration worked to prevent the crisis from escalating into a wider war. 1. Gaza hostage negotiations stalled as regional tensions escalated According to McGurkâs account in The Atlantic, Biden had asked him shortly after Hamasâs October 7, 2023, attack on Israel to help negotiate a cease-fire and hostage-release agreement. The first breakthrough came in November 2023, when a seven-day truce resulted in the release of more than 100 Israeli hostages, including women and children, in exchange for hundreds of Palestinian prisoners held by Israel. Humanitarian assistance also entered Gaza during the pause in fighting, McGurk wrote. However, negotiations collapsed on December 1 after Hamas refused to release younger women hostages as agreed and instead proposed moving directly to discussions over older male captives. Israel rejected the proposal, and fighting resumed. McGurk said Hamas subsequently demanded a return to the pre-October 7 status quo, including retaining control over Gaza. Israel, under Netanyahu, rejected the possibility of Hamas continuing to govern the territory. By February 2024, the war had entered its fifth month, with nearly 30,000 Palestinians reported killed, including militants, according to the figures cited by McGurk. More than 230 Israeli soldiers had also died, while Hamas continued to hold over 100 hostages. 2. Iranian-backed attacks on US forces pushed Washington towards confrontation While Washington attempted to revive hostage negotiations, attacks by Iranian-backed militias against American forces in Iraq and Syria intensified. McGurk wrote that attacks against US troops had increased sevenfold since October 7 compared with the previous year, with several strikes aimed at killing American personnel. On Christmas Day 2023, three US personnel were wounded in an attack in northern Iraq, one of them seriously. Days later, Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi group began targeting commercial shipping and military vessels in the Red Sea. According to McGurk, Biden subsequently asked him to meet Iranian representatives in Oman through an existing diplomatic back channel. The meeting was intended to communicate Washington's concerns and prevent further escalation. However, the diplomatic effort failed to produce an agreement. On January 28, 2024, an Iranian-supplied drone struck the living quarters of American troops in Jordan, killing three US soldiers and injuring dozens. Biden responded by ordering what McGurk described as the largest wave of American air strikes across Iraq and Syria in more than a decade. The strikes targeted militia infrastructure, including the leader held responsible for the Jordan attack and an Iranian adviser in Baghdad who was supporting the militias. McGurk said the militias subsequently stopped attacking American forces. 3. Biden attempted to bridge differences between Israel and Hamas In February 2024, McGurk returned to Cairo to revive the hostage negotiations with Egypt's intelligence chief Abbas Kamel and Israeli negotiators led by Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar. According to McGurk's account, the discussions initially appeared to have little chance of success because Israel and Hamas maintained fundamentally different positions. Hamas, through its leadership in Gaza, demanded a complete Israeli withdrawal, a permanent cease-fire and the release of all Palestinian prisoners in Israeli jails. Israel rejected these conditions. McGurk and CIA Director William Burns subsequently developed a compromise proposal focused on releasing a humanitarian category of hostages, including women, elderly people and the sick or wounded, in exchange for Palestinian prisoners. The proposal covered more than 30 hostages, including three Americans. In return, Hamas would receive a cease-fire lasting at least six weeks, with the possibility of extending it while negotiations continued over the remaining captives. Israeli negotiator Ronen Bar indicated that Israel could accept the broad framework, McGurk wrote. However, Egyptian intelligence chief Kamel warned that Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was unlikely to agree. The negotiations eventually stalled again, with Hamas rejecting the proposed compromise and maintaining its original demands. 4. Netanyahu's Rafah offensive threatened to deepen the crisis McGurk's account describes how Israel's preparations for a major offensive in Rafah, southern Gaza, became another obstacle to negotiations. During the February Cairo meeting, Bar informed the mediators that Israel was preparing its largest military operation of the war in Rafah. According to McGurk, Israeli intelligence believed Hamas remained militarily organised in the area, with brigades, battalions and an extensive tunnel network. Rafah was also sheltering large numbers of Palestinians displaced by Israeli military operations elsewhere in Gaza. Bar argued that the only way to stop the planned offensive was for Hamas to begin releasing hostages. During a subsequent meeting in Jerusalem, Netanyahu told McGurk that Hamas's continued presence near Israel's borders posed an existential security concern. The Israeli prime minister also indicated that if a Gaza agreement could not be reached, Israel might consider military action against Hezbollah in Lebanon to secure its northern border. McGurk wrote that Netanyahu was primarily focused on eliminating Hamas's military capabilities and believed that continued military pressure would eventually force Sinwar to release the hostages. The US negotiator, however, remained concerned that military escalation could further complicate the hostage negotiations. 5. US-Israel tensions intensified over the Gaza war By March 2024, Biden was facing growing domestic political pressure over Israel's military operations and the humanitarian situation in Gaza. According to McGurk, the president was under criticism from sections of his own Democratic Party for continuing military support to Israel. Earlier that month, Biden described Israel's planned Rafah operation as a âred lineâ in an interview, saying Israel âmust pay more attention to the innocent lives being lost.â Vice President Kamala Harris also described the proposed Rafah operation as a âhuge mistakeâ and did not rule out consequences if Israel proceeded. However, McGurk wrote that Biden later clarified that his comments concerned how Israel conducted the operation, rather than whether it should take place. The growing differences between Washington and Jerusalem coincided with the collapse of hostage negotiations. On March 18, Biden called Netanyahu and urged him to offer more Palestinian prisoners as part of the proposed agreement. Netanyahu reluctantly agreed, but Hamas did not change its position, according to McGurk. The United States subsequently abstained from a United Nations Security Council vote on a resolution calling for an unconditional cease-fire in Gaza during Ramadan, allowing it to pass. McGurk said Hamas viewed the resolution as a diplomatic opportunity and used Israel's growing international isolation to reinforce its negotiating position. Israeli negotiators eventually withdrew from the talks. 6. Israel's Damascus strike brought Iran and Israel closer to direct confrontation The crisis took a new turn on April 1, 2024, when Israel launched an air strike in Damascus, killing senior Iranian military commander Mohammad Reza Zahedi and several associates. According to McGurk, Zahedi was a senior Iranian officer responsible for proxy operations across Syria and Lebanon, including support for Hezbollah. Before the attack, Israeli military officials had informed McGurk that the operation was imminent. One Israeli official also warned that Iran might describe the targeted building as a consulate, although Israel maintained that it had no evidence that the facility was a diplomatic mission. After the strike, Iran declared that it considered the attack an assault on Iranian territory and vowed retaliation against Israel. McGurk wrote that American intelligence subsequently began receiving reports of Iranian preparations for a large-scale missile and drone attack against Israeli cities. The potential scale of the retaliation alarmed Washington. Iran had traditionally relied on regional proxy groups to confront Israel and the United States, allowing Tehran to maintain some distance from direct military confrontation. However, the planned attack appeared to represent a departure from that approach. According to McGurk, US officials assessed that Iran was preparing to launch hundreds of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones towards Israel. 7. Biden approved US military deployment despite deteriorating ties with Netanyahu As Iran's preparations became clearer, Israel formally requested American military assistance to defend its territory. McGurk described the request as extraordinary because it departed from Israel's traditional military doctrine: We defend ourselves, by ourselves. Israel sought American assistance involving air wings, destroyers and missile-defence systems. At the same time, Biden's relationship with Netanyahu was deteriorating. McGurk wrote that the two leaders had spoken only a handful of times during the first quarter of 2024, compared with nearly 20 conversations during the final quarter of 2023. The relationship further deteriorated after Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer called for elections in Israel and Netanyahu's replacement. Against this backdrop, Biden held a meeting with senior advisers, including Secretary of State Antony Blinken, CIA Director William Burns and national security adviser Jake Sullivan, on April 4. According to McGurk, Biden approved the emergency deployment of additional American military forces to the region on the recommendation of Defence Secretary Lloyd Austin. The president also discussed whether the United States should threaten to suspend military assistance to Israel to pressure Netanyahu into ending the Gaza war. However, Biden questioned the consequences of such a move while Israel faced attacks from multiple directions and hostages remained in Hamas captivity. âWeâre on the side of Iran?â he asked rhetorically, according to McGurk. 8. Biden confronted Netanyahu and linked Iran's defence to ending the Gaza war During the April 4 telephone conversation with Netanyahu, Biden expressed frustration over Israel's handling of the humanitarian crisis and the continuing military campaign in Gaza. According to McGurk, the president opened the call by asking: âBibi, man, what the fuck are you doing?â Biden warned that the United States could withdraw military assistance, while Netanyahu responded that Israel would defend itself even without American support. The discussion also covered the killing of seven World Central Kitchen aid workers in an Israeli drone strike in northern Gaza on April 1. Biden demanded concrete steps to improve humanitarian access, including opening additional crossings into northern Gaza. When Netanyahu attempted to explain Israel's preliminary assessment of the incident, Biden interrupted him. âI donât want to hear it, Bibi.â According to McGurk, Biden then made clear that the United States would help defend Israel against Iran but expected immediate efforts to end the Gaza war and secure the release of hostages. âThatâs the deal, pal.â Following the call, the White House issued a statement warning that US policy would be determined by its assessment of Israel's immediate actions regarding civilian harm, humanitarian suffering and the safety of aid workers. At the same time, the statement reaffirmed American support for Israel against Iranian threats. McGurk described this as the central dilemma confronting the Biden administration: Washington wanted to pressure Israel over Gaza without weakening its defence against Iran. 9. US-led multinational military operation intercepted Iran's unprecedented attack On April 13, 2024, Iran launched its first direct large-scale attack against Israel from its own territory. According to McGurk's account, the attack began at approximately 3:30 pm with around 200 drones, followed roughly 90 minutes later by 30 cruise missiles. Iran subsequently launched more than 100 ballistic missiles in multiple waves. The attack was designed to overwhelm Israeli air defences by ensuring that drones, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles arrived around the same time, McGurk wrote. The United States had spent the preceding 96 hours strengthening Israel's defences, deploying additional military assets and coordinating with Arab and European countries. During the attack, American fighter aircraft intercepted Iranian drones over Syria, Iraq and Saudi Arabia, while US Navy destroyers and regional air-defence systems helped counter incoming threats. McGurk described how US and Israeli defence systems worked together to intercept the incoming projectiles. Israel's Arrow systems engaged ballistic missiles at high altitudes, while American destroyers fired SM-3 interceptors to destroy incoming threats above the atmosphere. US Army Patriot batteries across the Middle East were also placed on alert. According to McGurk, American pilots Lieutenant Colonel Kevin Murphy and Major George Welton, along with their squadron, shot down around two dozen Iranian drones. The operation involved American military forces working alongside Israeli forces and a coalition of European and Arab countries. As the attack unfolded, General Erik Kurilla, who was overseeing US military operations, informed Biden that the number of ballistic missiles launched had increased through successive waves. McGurk recalled that the Situation Room tracked more than 100 Iranian ballistic missiles heading towards Israel. Despite the scale of the attack, the combined air-defence effort appeared to have prevented major damage. US military officials initially reported no confirmed impacts, while Israeli authorities subsequently reported no significant impacts. McGurk noted that one young girl in southern Israel was wounded by falling shrapnel. The successful interception prevented the immediate military consequences that could have triggered an Israeli retaliatory strike against Iran. 10. Biden urged Netanyahu to avoid retaliation and contain the conflict Following the interception operation, the immediate challenge for Washington was preventing Israel from launching a major retaliatory attack against Iran. According to McGurk, Biden wanted Netanyahu to recognise the success of the defensive operation and avoid turning it into a broader military confrontation. The president asked for Netanyahu to be brought onto a telephone call. When Netanyahu initially requested 30 minutes before speaking, Biden expressed frustration, asking whether the Israeli prime minister understood that the United States had just helped save Israel. National Security Adviser Jake Sullivan and his deputy Jon Finer subsequently prepared talking points recommending that Israel respond in a way that inflicted few casualties and prevented further escalation. During the conversation, Biden acknowledged Israel's right to respond but urged Netanyahu to coordinate with Washington and ensure that any action was designed to deter Iran rather than escalate the conflict. âTake the win,â Biden said. Netanyahu remained noncommittal, arguing that Iran needed to be taught a lesson. However, both leaders agreed that their military teams would discuss possible responses. McGurk wrote that the Biden administration subsequently received another warning from Tehran against supporting Israel in a retaliatory operation. Iran's UN mission also issued a public message stating: âUS MUST STAY AWAY!!â The immediate confrontation eventually subsided, although tensions between Israel and Iran continued. The following morning, Biden spoke with the American pilots and military commanders involved in defending Israel, including Murphy and Welton's squadron. Recalling the operation, Biden told the pilots: âThe only reason weâre not in a major war right now is because of what you did. I mean it, guys. Thank you, thank you, thank you. You saved the world; I mean it. God bless you.â According to McGurk, the episode demonstrated how American military coordination, regional cooperation and direct diplomatic engagement helped prevent Iran's unprecedented attack from triggering a wider regional war. However, the underlying Gaza conflict, stalled hostage negotiations and tensions between Washington and Jerusalem remained unresolved. This article is based on Brett McGurk's first-person account published in The Atlantic, adapted from his forthcoming bookBrink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages. title: Odisha chief electoral officer RS Gopalan seeks voluntary retirement
text: RS Gopalan, the Odisha Chief Electoral Officer, has applied for voluntary retirement from service. BHUBANESWAR: Odisha cadre IAS officer RS Gopalan, currently serving as Odishaâs chief electoral officer (CEO), on Wednesday applied for voluntary retirement from service. The move comes amid heightened scrutiny of the Election Commission of India over special intensive revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. However, Gopalan said his decision was unrelated to the exercise. âI have submitted my papers for personal and health reasons. I want to focus on certain personal matters,â Gopalan told TOI. A 2001-batch IAS officer, Gopalan said he had been contemplating leaving the service for several months but chose to wait until smooth completion of the SIR process and the final publication of the electoral rolls in Odisha. After SIR, Odishaâs electoral roll of 3.16 crore voters was published on Sept 21 with opposition BJD and Congress questioning the deletion of around 17 lakh voters. Tamil Nadu-born Gopalan had about a year-and-a-half service remaining. Sources said he is likely to stay in Odisha for around two years to allow his son to complete his schooling before deciding on his future plans. Gopalan has served as Odisha CEO since July 2024. During his 25-year career, he has held several key positions, including deputy director-general of the Unique Identification Authority of India (UIDAI), labour department secretary and agriculture director, among other assignments. title: HC frames 12 issues in Kantabanji BJP MLA election case
text: Orissa high court Cuttack : Orissa high court has framed 12 issues for adjudication in an election petition filed by a voter challenging the election of BJP MLA Laxman Bag from Kantabanji assembly constituency. Former Odisha chief minister and BJD supremo Naveen Patnaik was defeated by 16,344 votes in June 2024. Justice R K Pattanaik framed the issues on Sept 24, including allegations of irregularities in Bagâs nomination papers and disclosures made in the mandatory Form-26 affidavit. The court fixed 2 pm on Oct 9 for recording of evidence. The election petition was filed on July 18, 2024, by Kantabanji voter Giriraj Singh Majhi. The high court had admitted the petition on Aug 5, 2024. Majhi has sought annulment of Bagâs election, alleging that his nomination was improperly accepted despite alleged non-compliance with the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and Conduct of Elections Rules, 1961. A key focus of the election case proceedings will be Form-26, the affidavit that a candidate is required to submit along with the nomination papers. It contains information for voters about the candidate, including pending criminal cases, assets and liabilities, educational qualifications and other prescribed disclosures. The court will examine whether Bag furnished the required affidavit and whether the information disclosed in it was complete and correct. Among the issues framed, the court will determine whether Bag filed his nomination with the requisite Form-26 affidavit, whether submission of photocopies of the affidavit amounted to a substantial defect and whether any such defect warranted rejection of his nomination. The court will also check allegations that Bag suppressed or falsely declared information concerning pending criminal cases, his and his spouseâs movable and immovable assets, the separate bank account for election expenditure and his educational qualification. Another issue is whether the returning officer illegally or improperly accepted Bagâs nomination and, if so, whether this materially affected the election result. The court will further consider whether Bagâs election should be declared void for alleged non-compliance with Section 33A of the RP Act read with Rule 4A of the Conduct of Election Rules and Form-25. The maintainability of the election petition is also among the issues. title: Rubio urges Cuba to 'choose a different path', warns of consequences for resisting Trump
text: Trump previously expressed his intention to change Cuba's communist government (Photo: AP). US secretary of state Marco Rubio said Washington hopes Cuba will choose "a different path" from communism, warning the Cuban government to recognise the consequences of failing to change course. "We are hopeful that Cuba will choose a different path," Rubio told Fox News, adding that he hoped "some people" controlling the Cuban government would "open their eyes to the reality of what they are facing." US President Donald Trump has previously expressed his intention to change Cuba's communist government. Rubio also warned those who believe they can wait out the Trump administration that they would "learn the lesson the hard way" if they refuse to change course. "Unfortunately, the people that continue there to chant revolutionary slogans, too many of them still believe that they could wait out this administration and make no changes or do nothing," Rubio said. Speaking at the UN General Assembly on Saturday, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez said Havana would always remain open to dialogue with Washington. Over the weekend, Trump predicted that the US and Cuba would reach an agreement and said he did not believe military action would be necessary. The US has maintained an embargo on Cuba for more than 60 years, while the Trump administration has increased pressure on Havana. This has included actions against Venezuela, where the US military removed and seized former president Nicolas Maduro in January. An oil blockade imposed by the US earlier this year has put further strain on Cuba as the island grapples with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by deteriorating infrastructure. Turning to Venezuela in the same interview, Rubio said the country "need[s] to have free and fair elections". title: Amrinder Singh Raja Warring seeks SIR suspension in Punjab till assembly polls
text: Chandigarh: Punjab Congress president Amrinder Singh Raja Warring today demanded suspension of Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the electoral rolls in Punjab till the next assembly elections scheduled in six months from now. He also demanded that the elections should be conducted based on the existing electoral rolls, which were made the base for the 2024 General Elections, without any deletions. He said this was the only way to ensure that no genuine voter is denied the precious right to vote. The PCC president disclosed that thousands of genuine and deserving first-time voters were being denied the franchise due to the severe complexities in the new âForm-6â, which they need to fill up for registering as voters. He demanded that the provision of reference to their (first time votersâ) parents or grandparents in the previous electoral roll is the most difficult condition to fill. Warring said that while Congress party has persistently been maintaining that SIR in its current form was nothing but a blatant and unabashed attempt to âdisfranchiseâ lakhs of voters, whom BJP suspects not to be its supporters, the recent revelations have only vindicated the partyâs apprehensions. âThis has shaken the faith of the people in the fairness of elections,â he remarked. He said while the draft electoral rolls for Punjab are yet to be released, there are indications and apprehensions that the names of lakhs of voters are being deleted from the electoral rolls. âThis will be the travesty of justice and electoral democracy that a large section of voters is disenfranchised just a few months ahead of the elections,â he said, while asserting that SIR should be suspended till the elections and carried out afterwards with due transparency and without any complexities. text: Guwahati: Aasu-backed candidate Arunav Duarah was elected president of Gauhati University Postgraduate Studentsâ Union (PGSU), as Aasu and Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad ( ABVP ) won most of the 18 posts in the studentsâ body.
